title: IIT Bombay Student's Death After ChatGPT Exam Incident Sparks Protests and Police FIR
excerpt: Second-year student Sahil Wakode was found dead in his Powai hostel hours after being caught using a phone in an exam; 400-plus students protested, exams were postponed, and police have registered an FIR.
body:
• Sahil Ravindra Wakode, a 22-year-old second-year BTech student from Maharashtra's Yavatmal district, was found dead in his IIT Bombay hostel room on Friday evening, hours after being caught using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination.
  • The institute says Wakode had allegedly uploaded the question paper to ChatGPT to seek answers, but insists no disciplinary action was initiated and that he was counselled and assured his academic career would not be affected.
  • Mumbai Police first registered an accidental death report and, on Saturday, an FIR against people linked to the exam incident; more than 400 students staged late-night protests demanding transparency, and mid-semester examinations were postponed.
  • The death is the third reported student suicide at the Powai campus in roughly seven months, renewing scrutiny of disciplinary procedures and mental-health support at the country's premier engineering institutes.

Sahil Ravindra Wakode, a second-year BTech student in the Department of Energy Science and Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, was found dead in his hostel room on the Powai campus on Friday evening, hours after he was caught using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination, according to officials and a statement from the institute. His mother has demanded justice, alleging her son was mistreated. The death has triggered campus-wide protests and a police investigation.

Wakode, 22, was found in his room in Hostel Number 4 after his hostel mates received no response and alerted the authorities, who then informed the police, an official said. No suicide note was recovered from the room, and the body has been sent for post-mortem examination. Powai police initially registered an accidental death report. On Saturday, officials said an FIR had been registered against all persons linked to the exam incident, and the student's phone and campus CCTV footage were seized as evidence.

Exam hall confrontation

According to IIT Bombay's statement, Wakode was found using a mobile phone in the examination hall earlier on Friday, and had allegedly uploaded the examination question paper to an AI platform — identified by other reports as ChatGPT — to seek answers during the test. The institute said the examination instructor and the Head of the Department discussed the matter with the student, counselled him, and assured him the incident would not adversely affect his academic career. No disciplinary proceedings were initiated, the institute stated.

Wakode then returned to his hostel room. He was found dead later that evening.

The institute expressed grief over the death and said it was extending support to the student's friends, classmates, faculty members and others affected by the tragedy, adding that the circumstances were being examined by the appropriate authorities.

"My son was killed, tortured. I want justice."

— Wakode's mother, speaking to PTI

Campus erupts in protest

The death triggered late-night protests on campus, with reports saying more than 400 students gathered to demand transparency and accountability from the administration. The student's parents also joined the protest, calling for an explanation from the institute, according to reports. The ongoing mid-semester examinations were postponed amid the unrest.

At the centre of the dispute is a sharp divide between the institute's account and allegations from protesting students. Some students alleged that Wakode had been threatened with a one-year suspension over the examination incident — a step they said could have forced him to vacate his hostel and delay his degree. IIT Bombay has denied initiating any disciplinary proceedings, and the suspension claim has not been independently verified.

Police are recording the statements of the student's family, who have arrived in Mumbai, as well as statements from students on campus, officials said. Some media reports also said the case had been transferred to the Mumbai Crime Branch after the parents raised claims of caste-based discrimination — a charge the authorities have not yet publicly addressed.

Third death in seven months

The death is the third reported case of suicide at the IIT Bombay campus in Powai in roughly seven months, according to reports. In February, a second-year student died by suicide in a hostel, and in July 2026, at the beginning of the new semester, a 20-year-old second-year BTech student also ended his life.

The pattern has intensified a national conversation about academic pressure, disciplinary processes and mental-health services at India's elite institutions, where admission is fiercely competitive and the stakes of a single examination can feel overwhelming. Students involved in the protest argued that suspension rules — which can force hostel eviction and delayed graduation — compound the fear around any disciplinary incident, regardless of what the administration says about counselling.

What the investigation will decide

The post-mortem report, the findings from Wakode's seized phone and the CCTV footage, and the outcome of the police probe will be critical in establishing what transpired in the hours between the examination confrontation and his death. The administration has said it will support the inquiry; students want a formal, transparent account of the events that led to it.

For now, the Powai campus remains unsettled — and the institute faces uncomfortable questions about whether its procedures for handling academic misconduct account for the psychological toll they can exact on young students far from home.
image_caption: The main gate of the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay in Powai, Mumbai, with a Mumbai Police constable on duty. Powai police have registered an FIR against people linked to the exam incident after the death of second-year student Sahil Wakode.
nri_angle: The case lands hard on diaspora families whose children study at or aspire to India's elite institutes — it raises urgent questions about campus mental-health support and disciplinary pressure.
